themes.summary: No paper read in full states that a chance setback caused by one specific outside party (lawsuit, fraud, failing supplier, departing partner, shrinking client) is a kind of trigger; the closest are Kirtley and O'Mahony's case of a manufacturing partner that failed to deliver, Harmeling and Sarasvathy's rejections by others as negative contingencies, and Dew's remark that unlucky incidents can be the contingent part of serendipity. themes.summary: Liu and Tsay (2024) state that chance negative shocks force young firms to exit, and Brownell et al. (2024) state that venture failure comes from mistake, misfortune or both, so a purely harmful role for chance events is stated; Kirtley and O'Mahony (2023) add that firms sometimes absorb a problem's negative impact without changing direction. The serendipity papers themselves (Dew, Busch) only lean on it, since they treat unlucky events as possible inflection points rather than as pure setbacks.

searches.query: grep setback|adversit|blessing|misfortune|bad luck|reframe|turned out across papers/md
searches.note: Brownell read in full; it states the bad-luck-later-reframed-as-good-luck idea in its limitations section, flagged by the authors as going beyond their data. Sarasvathy (2008) lemonade principle and Harmeling and Sarasvathy (2013) are about acting on contingencies, not retelling them; not quoted. Garud et al (2014) treats setbacks as a threat to legitimacy, not as retold fortune.

themes.summary: Brownell et al (2024), read in full, states the idea: a venture that capitalises on an event first seen as bad luck might later reframe it as good luck, though the authors say this conjecture goes beyond their data. Liu and Tsay (2024), Cunha et al (2010) and Tesfaye et al (2026) lean on it, and the failure-narrative papers that might state it outright are abstract only.

themes.summary: Stated: Buenstorf (2007) says existing firms create opportunities, some serendipitous, that employees pursue in spinoffs, and Garud et al. (2011) and Busch & Grimes (2023) describe employees inside a firm stumbling onto discoveries and using company resources to develop them. Shah & Tripsas (2007) add that spinoff founders carry status and resources from their parent firm, so a background code for an existing firm's ideas, staff, or resources has paper backing.
